Consider implementing Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) to restrict DLL loading to signed binaries.

title: Privilege Escalation: Dangerous Token Privileges
description: The current process or service accounts hold dangerous Windows token privileges. SeImpersonatePrivilege and SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege enable token impersonation attacks (Potato family exploits). SeDebugPrivilege allows debugging any process including LSASS. SeBackupPrivilege/SeRestorePrivilege bypass file ACLs. SeTcbPrivilege acts as part of the operating system.
impact: Token impersonation privileges (SeImpersonate, SeAssignPrimaryToken) enable immediate SYSTEM-level privilege escalation via tools like JuicyPotato, PrintSpoofer, RoguePotato, or GodPotato. SeDebugPrivilege allows LSASS memory dumping for credential extraction. These privileges are commonly held by IIS application pool accounts, SQL Server service accounts, and other service identities.
remediation_brief: Review and minimize token privileges assigned to service accounts. Remove SeImpersonatePrivilege and SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege from service accounts where not operationally required. Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) with minimal privileges. Audit User Rights Assignments via: secpol.msc > Local Policies > User Rights Assignment. Consider running services in Windows containers or AppContainers which restrict available privileges.

title: Privilege Escalation: Unquoted Service Path
description: One or more Windows services have unquoted executable paths containing spaces, AND at least one intermediate directory in the path is writable by non-administrative users. Windows resolves unquoted paths by trying each space-delimited segment as a potential executable.
impact: An attacker can place an executable at a space-boundary in the unquoted path. For example, if the service path is 'C:\Program Files\Some Service\service.exe' (unquoted), placing 'C:\Program.exe' or 'C:\Program Files\Some.exe' in a writable directory causes it to execute with the service's privileges. This requires both the unquoted path AND a writable intermediate directory to be exploitable.

mitre_attack.name: Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception by Unquoted Path

remediation_brief: Quote all service binary paths that contain spaces. Fix via registry: reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<ServiceName>" /v ImagePath /t REG_EXPAND_SZ /d '"C:\Program Files\...\service.exe"' /f. Additionally, restrict write permissions on all intermediate directories in service paths. Identify all unquoted paths: wmic service get name,pathname | findstr /i /v "C:\Windows" | findstr /i "  ".

title: Access Control: Named Pipe Permission Weakness
description: Named pipes on this system have overly permissive access controls, allowing non-administrative users to read, write, or impersonate connections on pipes used by privileged services.
impact: Improperly secured named pipes can be exploited for privilege escalation or lateral movement. An attacker can connect to a weakly-permissioned pipe to capture or relay authentication tokens, inject commands into service communication channels, or impersonate the pipe server's identity. Named pipe impersonation is a core technique in several Potato-family privilege escalation exploits.
remediation_brief: Audit named pipe ACLs using pipelist.exe (Sysinternals) and accesschk.exe. Restrict pipe permissions to the minimum required identities. Remove write/connect access for Authenticated Users and Everyone groups on privileged service pipes. Implement pipe security descriptors in service configurations.

title: Persistence: WMI Event Subscription
description: Active WMI event subscriptions (EventFilter + EventConsumer + FilterToConsumerBinding) were found on this system. WMI subscriptions execute automatically in response to system events and survive reboots, making them a powerful persistence mechanism.
impact: WMI event subscriptions run with SYSTEM privileges and are difficult to detect through standard monitoring. An attacker can use them to execute malicious scripts or binaries when specific events occur (user logon, process creation, time-based triggers). WMI persistence is used by APT groups and is notoriously resistant to removal — it survives reinstallation of applications and many cleanup procedures.

mitre_attack.name: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription

remediation_brief: Review all WMI event subscriptions: Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __EventFilter; Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __EventConsumer; Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __FilterToConsumerBinding. Remove any unknown or suspicious subscriptions. Deploy Sysmon with WMI monitoring (Event IDs 19-21). Implement WMI activity logging via Group Policy.

title: Persistence: COM Object Hijacking
description: COM object registrations in the HKCU registry hive override HKLM registrations for CLSIDs that are loaded by privileged processes. This COM object hijacking technique allows a user-level modification to cause a privileged process to load an attacker-controlled DLL.
impact: COM hijacking is a stealthy persistence and privilege escalation technique. When a legitimate, privileged application loads a hijacked CLSID, it executes the attacker's DLL with the application's privileges. This survives reboots, is difficult to detect without specific monitoring, and blends with normal COM activity. Many legitimate Windows processes load COM objects during startup.

mitre_attack.name: Event Triggered Execution: Component Object Model Hijacking

remediation_brief: Audit HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID for entries that shadow HKLM CLSID registrations. Remove unauthorized CLSID overrides. Deploy Sysmon with registry monitoring (Event IDs 12-14) targeting CLSID paths. Implement application whitelisting (AppLocker/WDAC) to prevent loading of unauthorized DLLs from user-writable locations.

title: Persistence: AppInit_DLLs Configured
description: The AppInit_DLLs registry value is configured with one or more DLL paths. Windows loads any DLL listed in AppInit_DLLs into every process that loads user32.dll — which includes virtually all GUI applications. This mechanism is a well-known persistence and injection technique.
impact: DLLs specified in AppInit_DLLs are loaded into every GUI process on the system, providing system-wide code injection. An attacker can use this for keylogging, credential interception, API hooking, or persistent backdoor access. The injected DLL runs with the privileges of each host process, potentially including SYSTEM-level services.
remediation_brief: Clear the AppInit_DLLs registry value: reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows" /v AppInit_DLLs /f. Also clear the WOW64 key: reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows" /v AppInit_DLLs /f. Set LoadAppInit_DLLs to 0 to disable the mechanism entirely. Enable Secure Boot and RequireSignedAppInit_DLLs to restrict to signed DLLs only.

title: Persistence: IFEO Debugger Set
description: Image File Execution Options (IFEO) registry entries have a 'Debugger' value set for one or more executables. This causes Windows to launch the specified debugger program instead of (or before) the target executable, effectively hijacking the execution of legitimate programs.
impact: An attacker can set an IFEO debugger entry for commonly used programs (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, taskmgr.exe) to redirect their execution to a malicious binary. This is a stealthy persistence mechanism that activates whenever the legitimate program is launched. It is also used to prevent security tools from running by redirecting them to an empty program or a kill command.

mitre_attack.name: Event Triggered Execution: Image File Execution Options Injection

remediation_brief: Audit IFEO registry entries: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options" /s /v Debugger. Remove any unauthorized Debugger values. Deploy Sysmon with registry monitoring (Event IDs 12-14) targeting IFEO keys. Legitimate IFEO uses include application compatibility shims — verify with the application vendor before removing.

title: Persistence: Accessibility Feature Modified
description: One or more Windows accessibility feature binaries (sethc.exe, utilman.exe, osk.exe, narrator.exe, magnify.exe, DisplaySwitch.exe) have been modified or replaced. The modification timestamp does not align with the OS installation date or last Windows Update, indicating potential tampering.
impact: Replacing accessibility binaries with cmd.exe or a backdoor is a classic persistence technique that provides SYSTEM-level command prompt access from the Windows login screen — before any user has authenticated. An attacker can press Shift five times (sethc.exe), Win+U (utilman.exe), or similar shortcuts to trigger the backdoor. This survives reboots, user password changes, and most remediation attempts short of restoring the original binaries.
remediation_brief: Restore original accessibility binaries from a known-good source or Windows installation media: sfc /scannow or DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Verify file hashes against Microsoft published hashes. Investigate as a potential compromise — this finding indicates the system may have been backdoored. Deploy file integrity monitoring on %SystemRoot%\System32\sethc.exe, utilman.exe, osk.exe, narrator.exe, magnify.exe, DisplaySwitch.exe.

title: Persistence: Print Monitor DLL
description: Custom print monitor DLLs were found registered in the system. Print monitors are loaded by the Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe) which runs as SYSTEM. An unauthorized print monitor DLL provides persistent, SYSTEM-level code execution.
impact: Print monitor DLLs are loaded by the spoolsv.exe service at startup and run with SYSTEM privileges. An attacker who registers a malicious DLL as a print monitor achieves persistence that survives reboots and is difficult to detect — the DLL appears as a legitimate print subsystem component. This technique is used by APT groups for long-term persistence.

mitre_attack.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Port Monitors

remediation_brief: Audit print monitor registry entries: reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors" /s. Compare against known legitimate monitors (Standard TCP/IP Port, WSD Port, USB Monitor, Local Port). Remove any unknown or suspicious monitor entries. Verify DLL signatures for all registered monitor DLLs. Deploy Sysmon with registry monitoring on the Print\Monitors key.

title: Persistence: LSA Authentication Package Modified
description: Non-default authentication packages or security support providers (SSPs) are registered in the LSA registry configuration. LSA authentication packages are loaded by lsass.exe at boot and run with SYSTEM privileges. Unauthorized packages can intercept credentials during authentication.
impact: A malicious LSA authentication package runs inside lsass.exe with SYSTEM privileges and intercepts every authentication event on the system. This allows credential harvesting of all user passwords (including domain admin) in cleartext as they authenticate. This is one of the most powerful persistence mechanisms available, used by advanced threat actors and tools like mimilib.

mitre_attack.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Authentication Package

remediation_brief: Audit LSA registry entries: reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" /v "Authentication Packages" and "Security Packages". Default values are 'msv1_0' for Authentication Packages and '' (empty) or 'kerberos msv1_0 schannel wdigest tspkg pku2u' for Security Packages. Remove any unauthorized entries. Enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) to prevent unauthorized DLL loading into lsass.exe. Enable Credential Guard for additional protection. Investigate as potential compromise.

title: ADCS: ESC1 - Misconfigured Certificate Template
description: A certificate template allows enrollees to specify a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) in the certificate request, AND low-privileged users can enroll, AND the template has an EKU that permits authentication (Client Authentication, PKINIT, Smart Card Logon, or any purpose). This is the ESC1 attack vector identified by SpecterOps.
impact: Any low-privileged domain user can request a certificate with an arbitrary SAN (e.g., specifying a Domain Admin UPN). This certificate can then be used for Kerberos authentication as the impersonated user, achieving complete domain compromise without needing to know the target user's password. This is the most commonly exploited ADCS vulnerability.
remediation_brief: Disable 'Supply in the request' option on the Subject Name tab of vulnerable certificate templates. Instead, configure 'Build from Active Directory information'. Restrict enrollment permissions to only the users/groups that require the template. Remove unnecessary EKUs (especially 'Any Purpose'). Consider removing the template entirely if not operationally required. Audit with: certutil -v -template | findstr /i 'CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT'.

title: ADCS: ESC2 - Overly Permissive Template
description: A certificate template has an Extended Key Usage (EKU) of 'Any Purpose' (OID 2.5.29.37.0) or no EKU at all (which is equivalent to any purpose), AND low-privileged users can enroll. Certificates with Any Purpose or no EKU restrictions can be used for any purpose including client authentication, code signing, and subordinate CA issuance.
impact: A certificate with 'Any Purpose' or no EKU can be used for client authentication (impersonating any user), code signing (creating trusted malicious software), or even as a subordinate CA certificate (issuing arbitrary certificates). The combination of unrestricted EKU and broad enrollment permissions creates a powerful attack vector for domain compromise.
remediation_brief: Replace 'Any Purpose' EKU with specific, required EKUs only (e.g., Client Authentication only if that is the purpose). Remove templates with no EKU unless operationally justified. Restrict enrollment permissions to the minimum required groups. Audit all templates for overly broad EKU settings using certipy or Certutil.

title: ADCS: ESC3 - Enrollment Agent Template
description: A certificate template with the Certificate Request Agent EKU (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.1) allows low-privileged users to enroll. An Enrollment Agent certificate enables the holder to request certificates on behalf of other users, including privileged accounts.
impact: An attacker can first obtain an Enrollment Agent certificate, then use it to request certificates for any other user in the domain (e.g., Domain Admins) using a second template that allows enrollment by enrollment agents. This two-step attack achieves domain compromise by impersonating any user via certificate-based authentication.
remediation_brief: Restrict enrollment permissions on Enrollment Agent templates to only authorized Certificate Enrollment administrators. Configure enrollment restrictions on the CA: right-click CA > Properties > Enrollment Agents tab to restrict which enrollment agents can enroll for which templates and users. Consider disabling the Enrollment Agent template if not operationally required.

title: ADCS: ESC4 - Vulnerable Template ACL
description: A certificate template's access control list (ACL) grants write permissions (WriteDACL, WriteOwner, WriteProperty, or GenericWrite) to low-privileged users or groups. This allows an attacker to modify the template configuration to introduce ESC1-ESC3 conditions.
impact: An attacker with write access to a certificate template can modify it to enable ESC1 (add CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT), change EKUs to 'Any Purpose', or enable enrollment for their own account. After modification, they exploit the newly created ESC1/ESC2/ESC3 condition for domain compromise. The template modification itself may go unnoticed without specific ADCS auditing.
remediation_brief: Audit all certificate template ACLs and remove write permissions for non-administrative groups. Only Enterprise Admins, Domain Admins, and designated PKI administrators should have write access to templates. Use: certutil -v -template | Select-String 'Allow.*Write'. Review and tighten ACLs via certtmpl.msc. Enable ADCS auditing to detect template modifications.

title: ADCS: ESC6 - EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2
description: The Certificate Authority has the EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag enabled. This CA-level configuration allows ANY certificate requester to specify an arbitrary Subject Alternative Name (SAN) in their request, regardless of template settings. This effectively makes every authentication template on this CA vulnerable to ESC1.
impact: With this flag enabled, any domain user who can enroll in any template with an authentication EKU can specify an arbitrary SAN, impersonating any user in the domain including Domain Admins. This is a CA-wide misconfiguration that bypasses per-template SAN controls — fixing individual templates does not mitigate this issue. A single CA with this flag compromises the entire domain.
remediation_brief: Disable the EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag on the CA: certutil -config "CA\CAName" -setreg policy\EditFlags -EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2. Restart the CA service: net stop certsvc && net start certsvc. Verify: certutil -config "CA\CAName" -getreg policy\EditFlags — the output should NOT include EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2. After disabling, audit all recently issued certificates for suspicious SAN values.

title: ADCS: ESC8 - NTLM Relay to HTTP Enrollment
description: The AD Certificate Services web enrollment endpoint is accessible over HTTP (not HTTPS) and/or does not enforce Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA). This allows NTLM relay attacks where a coerced machine account authentication (e.g., via PetitPotam, PrinterBug) can be relayed to the enrollment endpoint to request a certificate as the machine.
impact: An attacker can coerce a domain controller to authenticate to their machine (using PetitPotam, PrinterBug, or similar), then relay that authentication to the ADCS HTTP enrollment endpoint to obtain a certificate as the DC's machine account. This certificate allows the attacker to authenticate as the DC, enabling DCSync to extract all domain credentials. This is a full domain compromise path.
remediation_brief: Enable HTTPS on all ADCS web enrollment endpoints and disable HTTP. Enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) in IIS: IIS Manager > Authentication > Windows Authentication > Advanced Settings > Extended Protection = Required. Alternatively, disable the web enrollment role entirely if not required and use certreq or autoenrollment instead. Install patches for PetitPotam (CVE-2021-36942). Enable NTLM relay mitigations: enable SMB signing, LDAP signing, and channel binding.

title: Endpoint Protection: Application Whitelisting Not Configured
description: Neither AppLocker nor Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) is configured on this system. Without application whitelisting, any executable, script, or DLL can run without restriction.
impact: Without application control, an attacker can execute arbitrary malware, scripts, and tools on the system without restriction. Application whitelisting is consistently rated as one of the most effective endpoint security controls by ACSC Essential Eight, NIST, and CIS. Its absence significantly increases the attack surface for malware execution, lateral movement tools, and post-exploitation frameworks.
remediation_brief: Implement AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC). Start in audit mode to identify legitimate applications, then switch to enforce mode. At minimum, implement script rules to block unauthorized script execution. For WDAC: create a base policy with Microsoft recommended block rules, then supplement with organization-specific allow rules. For AppLocker: configure default rules plus explicit allow rules for approved applications.

title: System Hardening: HVCI Not Enabled
description: Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI / Memory Integrity) is not enabled on this system. HVCI uses virtualization-based security (VBS) to protect the Windows kernel code integrity verification process, preventing kernel-mode code injection and driver-based attacks.
impact: Without HVCI, the kernel is vulnerable to code injection attacks via malicious drivers, kernel exploits, and rootkits. HVCI prevents unsigned or improperly signed kernel-mode code from executing, significantly raising the bar for kernel-level attacks. Its absence leaves the system vulnerable to bootkit/rootkit installations and kernel-mode exploit payloads.
remediation_brief: Enable HVCI via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Device Guard > Turn On Virtualization Based Security > Virtualization Based Protection of Code Integrity = Enabled with UEFI lock. Alternatively, enable via Windows Security > Device Security > Core isolation > Memory integrity. Prerequisites: compatible CPU with virtualization extensions (Intel VT-x/AMD-V), UEFI firmware, Secure Boot enabled.

title: System Hardening: CredSSP Delegation Enabled
description: Credential Security Support Provider (CredSSP) delegation is enabled, allowing this system to forward user credentials to remote servers. The AllowFreshCredentials or AllowFreshCredentialsDomain policies permit credential delegation to specified or all remote hosts.
impact: CredSSP delegation sends the user's cleartext credentials to the remote server. If the remote server is compromised, these credentials are immediately available to the attacker. CredSSP delegation to '*' (all servers) is especially dangerous as it enables credential forwarding to any host, including attacker-controlled machines. This defeats the purpose of Restricted Admin mode and other credential protection mechanisms.

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

remediation_brief: Disable CredSSP delegation via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Credentials Delegation > Allow delegating fresh credentials = Disabled. If CredSSP is required for specific administrative tasks, restrict delegation to specific trusted servers only (never use '*'). Apply CVE-2018-0886 patches. Consider using Remote Credential Guard instead of CredSSP for RDP sessions.

title: Endpoint Protection: AMSI Not Registered
description: No Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) provider is registered on this system. AMSI is a Windows interface that allows applications to send content (scripts, macro code, .NET assemblies) to the installed antimalware solution for scanning before execution.
impact: Without AMSI, script-based attacks (PowerShell, VBScript, JScript, .NET) can execute malicious code without real-time scanning. AMSI is the primary defense against fileless malware, obfuscated scripts, and in-memory attacks. Its absence or deregistration is a common attacker technique (T1562.001) to disable defenses before deploying payloads.

mitre_attack.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

remediation_brief: Verify that Windows Defender or a third-party antimalware solution with AMSI support is installed and active. Check AMSI provider registration: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\AMSI\Providers" /s. If no providers are listed, reinstall or re-register the antimalware solution. If AMSI was deliberately tampered with, investigate as a potential compromise indicator.

title: System Hardening: .NET Framework v2/v3.5 Installed
description: .NET Framework version 2.0 or 3.5 is installed on this system. These legacy .NET versions include the CLR v2 runtime which has weaker security controls than CLR v4 and can be leveraged by attackers to bypass application-level security restrictions.
impact: The .NET CLR v2 runtime can be invoked by PowerShell v2 and other tools to bypass AMSI, script block logging, constrained language mode, and other security controls that are only enforced in CLR v4. Attackers specifically target legacy .NET to downgrade the runtime and evade security monitoring. If .NET 2.0/3.5 is not required by any application, it represents unnecessary attack surface.
remediation_brief: Remove .NET Framework 3.5 (includes 2.0 and 3.0) if no application requires it: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName NetFx3. On Server: Remove-WindowsFeature NET-Framework-Core. Before removing, verify no application dependencies by auditing installed software and testing in a pre-production environment.

title: System Hardening: PS Constrained Language Not Enforced
description: PowerShell is running in Full Language Mode rather than Constrained Language Mode (CLM). Full Language Mode allows unrestricted access to .NET types, COM objects, and Win32 APIs, enabling powerful post-exploitation capabilities.
impact: Full Language Mode enables attackers to load arbitrary .NET assemblies, invoke Win32 APIs via P/Invoke or Add-Type, create COM objects, and execute complex exploitation frameworks (Invoke-Mimikatz, PowerView, etc.) entirely in memory. Constrained Language Mode blocks these capabilities while preserving administrative scripting functionality.
remediation_brief: Enforce Constrained Language Mode via WDAC/AppLocker code integrity policies (the most robust method — CLM activates automatically when UMCI is enforced). Alternatively, set the __PSLockdownPolicy environment variable to 4 (system-wide), though this is less robust than WDAC enforcement. Test with administrative scripts first — CLM restricts .NET and COM access that some admin scripts require.

title: System Hardening: ASR Rules Not Configured
description: Windows Defender Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules are not configured or are set to audit-only mode. ASR rules block specific behaviors commonly used by malware, such as Office macros creating child processes, obfuscated scripts, credential theft from LSASS, and untrusted USB process execution.
impact: Without ASR rules, the system lacks behavioral protection against common attack techniques: Office macro malware, script-based attacks, credential dumping, ransomware file encryption patterns, and lateral movement techniques. ASR rules are one of the most effective free security controls available on Windows 10/11 and Server 2016+.
remediation_brief: Enable ASR rules via Group Policy or Intune. Recommended rules to enable in block mode: Block Office apps from creating child processes (D4F940AB-401B-4EFC-AADC-AD5F3C50688A), Block credential stealing from LSASS (9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2), Block executable content from email/webmail (BE9BA2D9-53EA-4CDC-84E5-9B1EEEE46550), Use advanced protection against ransomware (c1db55ab-c21a-4637-bb3f-a12568109d35). Start in audit mode for 2 weeks, then switch to block.

title: Endpoint Protection: Controlled Folder Access Not Enabled
description: Windows Defender Controlled Folder Access is not enabled. This feature protects designated folders (Documents, Desktop, Pictures, etc.) from unauthorized modification by untrusted applications, serving as anti-ransomware protection.
impact: Without Controlled Folder Access, ransomware and destructive malware can freely encrypt or delete files in user profile folders and other protected locations. CFA provides a last line of defense against ransomware by blocking unauthorized write operations, even from elevated processes, unless the application is explicitly whitelisted.
remediation_brief: Enable Controlled Folder Access via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Microsoft Defender Antivirus > Microsoft Defender Exploit Guard > Controlled Folder Access > Configure Controlled folder access = Enabled (Block mode). Alternatively: Set-MpPreference -EnableControlledFolderAccess Enabled. Whitelist legitimate applications that need write access to protected folders.

title: Endpoint Protection: Network Protection Not Enabled
description: Windows Defender Network Protection is not enabled. Network Protection extends SmartScreen capabilities to block outbound connections to low-reputation or malicious domains and IP addresses, protecting against phishing, exploit hosting sites, and command-and-control infrastructure.
impact: Without Network Protection, the system can establish connections to known-malicious domains, phishing sites, and C2 infrastructure without being blocked. This feature provides network-layer defense against web-based threats and can prevent initial access (drive-by downloads, phishing), malware download, and C2 communication.
remediation_brief: Enable Network Protection via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Microsoft Defender Antivirus > Microsoft Defender Exploit Guard > Network Protection > Prevent users and apps from accessing dangerous websites = Enabled (Block mode). Alternatively: Set-MpPreference -EnableNetworkProtection Enabled. Start in audit mode to identify false positives before enforcing.

title: Endpoint Protection: Exploit Protection Not Configured
description: Windows Exploit Protection (successor to EMET) process mitigations are not configured. Exploit Protection applies per-process exploit mitigations such as DEP, ASLR, CFG (Control Flow Guard), heap integrity validation, and image load restrictions to protect against memory corruption exploits.
impact: Without process-level exploit mitigations, applications are more vulnerable to memory corruption exploits (buffer overflows, use-after-free, ROP chains). Exploit Protection mitigations make exploit development significantly harder and can prevent known exploitation techniques from succeeding, even against unpatched vulnerabilities.
remediation_brief: Configure Exploit Protection system-wide and per-application: Windows Security > App & browser control > Exploit protection settings. Enable for high-risk applications (browsers, Office, PDF readers, Java). Key mitigations: DEP (AlwaysOn), ASLR (ForceRelocateImages, BottomUp), CFG (enabled), SEHOP (enabled). Deploy via Group Policy using an XML configuration file: Set-ProcessMitigation -PolicyFilePath exploit-protection-settings.xml.

title: Active Directory: LAPS Not Deployed
description: Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) is not deployed on this system or in the domain. Without LAPS, local administrator passwords are typically identical across all machines in the domain, or are never rotated, or both.
impact: Shared local administrator passwords are the single most common lateral movement enabler in Active Directory environments. If one machine is compromised and its local admin password is recovered (via SAM dump, mimikatz, or other means), the same password grants admin access to every other machine in the domain. LAPS solves this by setting a unique, randomly generated password on each machine and rotating it automatically.
remediation_brief: Deploy LAPS (or Windows LAPS in Server 2025/Windows 11). Steps: 1) Extend the AD schema for LAPS attributes (ms-Mcs-AdmPwd, ms-Mcs-AdmPwdExpirationTime or Windows LAPS equivalents), 2) Install the LAPS CSE (Client-Side Extension) via GPO or SCCM, 3) Configure the LAPS GPO with password complexity, length (14+ chars), and age (30 days), 4) Set ACLs on the OU to restrict who can read the LAPS password (authorized helpdesk/admin groups only).

title: Active Directory: krbtgt Key Not Rotated
description: The krbtgt account password has not been changed in an extended period (typically 180+ days). The krbtgt account is used to encrypt all Kerberos Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs) in the domain. If its key material is compromised, an attacker can forge Golden Tickets.
impact: A compromised krbtgt key enables Golden Ticket attacks, granting the attacker unrestricted access to any resource in the domain for the lifetime of the key. Kerberos maintains two most-recent krbtgt key versions — rotating the password invalidates the oldest one. Microsoft recommends rotating the krbtgt password at least every 180 days, and immediately after any suspected domain compromise.

mitre_attack.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket

remediation_brief: Rotate the krbtgt password using the Microsoft krbtgt reset script or manually via PowerShell (Reset-KrbtgtPassword). IMPORTANT: The krbtgt password must be reset TWICE (with a sufficient interval between resets, at least equal to the maximum ticket lifetime — typically 10 hours) to invalidate all existing TGTs. Schedule regular rotation every 180 days. After a suspected compromise, reset immediately (twice).

title: Account Management: Stale Domain Accounts
description: Domain user accounts were found that have not logged in for an extended period (90+ days) and are still enabled. Stale accounts represent dormant attack surface that attackers can target without triggering alerts tied to active users.
impact: Stale accounts are attractive targets for attackers because their compromise is less likely to be noticed — no legitimate user will report unexpected activity. These accounts may retain their original (potentially weak) passwords, group memberships, and access permissions. If any stale account has privileged access, it presents an unmonitored path to escalation.
remediation_brief: Implement a regular account review process (at least quarterly). Disable accounts inactive for 90+ days. Delete accounts inactive for 180+ days after confirming they are no longer needed. Automate with PowerShell: Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 | Disable-ADAccount. Audit disabled accounts for sensitive group memberships before deletion.

title: Active Directory: SID History Abuse Risk
description: User or group accounts with non-empty SID History attributes were found. SID History is a legitimate migration feature that preserves access to resources in a source domain after migration. However, SID History can be abused to inject arbitrary SIDs (including Domain Admins) into a user's token.
impact: An attacker who can modify the SID History attribute can inject the SID of a privileged group (e.g., Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins) into their own or another account's SID History. The injected SID is included in the user's Kerberos tickets and PAC, granting access to all resources the injected SID has permission to. This is a stealthy persistence technique because the user's group memberships appear normal.
remediation_brief: Audit all accounts with SID History: Get-ADUser -Filter 'SIDHistory -like "*"' -Properties SIDHistory | Select Name,SIDHistory. Remove SID History entries after domain migration is complete and verified: Set-ADUser -Identity <user> -Remove @{SIDHistory=<SID>}. Enable SID filtering on all trusts to prevent cross-domain SID History abuse. Monitor Event ID 4765 (SID History added) and Event ID 4766 (SID History add attempt failed).

title: Monitoring: Sysmon Not Installed
description: Sysmon (System Monitor) is not installed on this system. Sysmon provides detailed telemetry about process creation, network connections, file creation, registry modifications, WMI events, and other security-relevant activities that are essential for threat detection and incident response.
impact: Without Sysmon, the system lacks granular visibility into process execution (with command lines and parent process chains), network connections per-process, file creation timestamps and hashes, registry modifications, WMI activity, and named pipe operations. This severely limits the ability to detect and investigate malicious activity, lateral movement, and persistence mechanisms. Native Windows event logs lack the detail that Sysmon provides.
remediation_brief: Install Sysmon from Microsoft Sysinternals: sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i sysmonconfig.xml. Use a community-maintained configuration such as SwiftOnSecurity/sysmon-config or olafhartong/sysmon-modular as a starting point. Key event types to enable: Process creation (Event 1), Network connection (Event 3), File creation (Event 11), Registry modification (Event 13), WMI events (Events 19-21). Forward Sysmon logs to a SIEM for detection and alerting.

title: Service Hardening: PrintNightmare Vulnerable
description: The system is vulnerable to PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527 / CVE-2021-1675). The Print Spooler service is running AND the RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators registry key is not set to 1, or the NoWarningNoElevationOnInstall / UpdatePromptSettings Point-and-Print restriction keys are configured unsafely.
impact: PrintNightmare allows any authenticated user (local or remote) to execute arbitrary code with SYSTEM privileges by exploiting the Print Spooler service's driver installation functionality. This vulnerability was actively exploited in the wild and provides reliable remote code execution. On domain controllers, it enables immediate domain compromise. Multiple exploit variants exist in public tooling.

mitre_attack.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Print Processors

remediation_brief: 1) Install all PrintNightmare patches (KB5004945 and later cumulative updates). 2) Set RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators=1: reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers\PointAndPrint" /v RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f. 3) Set NoWarningNoElevationOnInstall=0 and UpdatePromptSettings=0 in the same key. 4) On servers that do not need printing, disable the Print Spooler service entirely: Stop-Service Spooler; Set-Service Spooler -StartupType Disabled. 5) On domain controllers, always disable Print Spooler.

title: Network Hardening: DNS Zone Transfer Allowed
description: The DNS server role is installed and zone transfers (AXFR) are allowed to any requestor, or are not restricted to specific secondary DNS servers. This allows any host to download the complete contents of DNS zones, including all hostnames, IP addresses, and service records.
impact: Unrestricted DNS zone transfers expose the entire internal DNS namespace to any attacker who can reach the DNS server. This provides a complete map of internal hosts, services, domain controllers, and other infrastructure without triggering typical detection mechanisms. The information enables targeted attacks against specific systems and services identified through the zone data.
remediation_brief: Restrict zone transfers to authorized secondary DNS servers only. In DNS Manager: right-click zone > Properties > Zone Transfers > uncheck 'Allow zone transfers' or select 'Only to the following servers' and list authorized secondaries. For AD-integrated zones, consider disabling zone transfers entirely and relying on AD replication. Verify with: nslookup > set type=AXFR > ls -d <domain>.
